analysis.one_liner: Creates a public Medicare-based health plan anyone can buy, alongside richer ACA subsidies and a cap on seniors' out-of-pocket costs.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat without action in three House committees since its introduction, with 5 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The Choose Medicare Act would create a 'Medicare Part E' public health plan that any U.S. resident could buy through the insurance exchanges, and that employers could offer to workers, competing with private insurance. It would set the plan's payment rates between what Medicare and private insurers pay, require participating doctors and hospitals to join, and extend Medicare's drug price negotiation to the new plan. Separately, it would make ACA subsidies more generous, boost cost-sharing help for lower-income enrollees, put an annual out-of-pocket cap on traditional Medicare, create a $30 billion state reinsurance fund, and strengthen government review of insurance rates.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and marketplace enrollees would gain a gold-level public option and larger premium subsidies, including for households above 400% of the poverty line. Lower-income enrollees would get much richer cost-sharing reductions. Seniors in traditional Medicare would gain a hard annual out-of-pocket limit starting at $6,700. Workers at small and large employers could enroll in the public plan, and anyone who loses a job could keep it. Enrollees who need abortion or other reproductive care could get it covered regardless of state bans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace enrollees, the uninsured, and seniors

how_it_helps.text: Establishes Medicare Part E public plans available to any U.S. resident in the individual, small group, and large group markets, offered through the ACA exchanges and to employers on a voluntary basis.

Each Part E plan must provide gold-level coverage of all essential health benefits plus everything Medicare covers, including abortions and other reproductive services, with a provision preempting state laws that would prohibit that coverage.
Anyone who enrolls in a Part E plan through an employer and later loses that job can keep the coverage regardless of whether other coverage is available.

Part E payment rates must be negotiated to fall, in aggregate, between Medicare rates and the average rates private exchange insurers pay, and all Medicare-participating providers are automatically in-network, with Medicare's balance-billing limits applying.
Medicare's prescription drug negotiation and related excise tax provisions would apply to drugs covered under Part E plans.

ACA premium tax credits would be based on gold-level rather than silver plans, eligibility would be extended above 400% of the poverty line, and cost-sharing reductions would be significantly enriched for households up to 400% of poverty.
Beginning in 2027, traditional Medicare would get an annual out-of-pocket cost-sharing cap starting at $6,700, indexed to medical inflation.

The bill appropriates $2 billion in startup funding and initial reserves for the public plans and $30 billion for fiscal years 2026-2028 for a state reinsurance and affordability fund to lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs.

Rate review under the Public Health Service Act would be strengthened to correct excessive, unjustified, or unfairly discriminatory rates through denial, modification, or consumer rebates, and would apply to grandfathered plans.
Employers that do not offer affordable, minimum-value coverage would have to refer full-time employees to exchange navigators, and the navigator program would get additional funding.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a government-run competitor selling gold-level coverage at Medicare-influenced rates. Hospitals and doctors would see the new plan pay less on average than private insurers pay. Drug makers would face Medicare-style price negotiation on Part E drugs. Taxpayers would fund the $2 billion in startup costs, initial claim reserves, and the $30 billion reinsurance fund, plus the cost of permanently extending and enriching ACA subsidies, which the Congressional Budget Office has not been asked to score here.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, drug makers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Part E premiums must fully finance the plan's benefits and administrative costs, so savings over private plans depend entirely on the negotiated rate schedule; if rates must keep provider networks adequate, the price advantage over private plans could be small.

The bill authorizes $2 billion in startup funding, open-ended initial reserves, and $30 billion over three years for reinsurance, and permanently extends enhanced subsidies beyond 400% of poverty, all federal spending without an offset in the bill text.

All Medicare-participating providers become participating providers for Part E automatically, which could strain network adequacy if the negotiated rates are substantially below private rates, and providers could respond by shifting costs elsewhere.
Expanding exchange eligibility and richer cost-sharing could draw enrollment from employer coverage over time, changing the employer-sponsored system that most working people currently rely on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the bill stacks several concrete gains: a gold-level public option, bigger subsidies, richer cost-sharing help, a senior out-of-pocket cap, and tougher rate review. The honest trade-offs are fiscal (tens of billions in new appropriations and permanent subsidy expansion, unscored in the text) and structural (a public plan whose affordability hinges on payment rates that the bill itself requires to be high enough to maintain provider networks). The design is more incremental than single-payer: it leaves private insurance in place and competes with it rather than replacing it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to three House committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or floor action.

narrative.text: H.R. 3911 was introduced in the House on June 11, 2025, by Rep. Jimmy Gomez.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce Committees.
The bill has 5 cosponsors, all Democrats.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — has been recorded on the bill since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no committee action, private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers avoid the new public competitor and the bill's rate and rate-review rules for now; consumers have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: insurers and drug makers

for.name: Rep. Jimmy Gomez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Choose Medicare Act and recruited the bill's cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Don Beyer, Jared Huffman, LaMonica McIver, and Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has no recorded opposition vote; its support is entirely Democratic (sponsor and 5 cosponsors, all D), and it has not advanced to a vote where partisan lines would be measured.

industries.note: A government-run gold-level plan sold on the same exchanges, and offered to employers, would directly compete with private plans, and the bill strengthens federal and state corrective action against insurer rates. Insurers' interest in blocking the bill runs against consumers who would gain a cheaper option.

Part E plans bring a new pool of insured patients and automatically include all Medicare-participating providers, but payment rates are capped at no more than average private exchange rates and balance billing is restricted, so revenue per patient would tend to be below private insurance.

Medicare's drug price negotiation and the associated excise tax for noncompliance would extend to drugs covered under Part E plans, and the bill encourages alternative payment models including for prescription drugs.

Employers could voluntarily offer a Part E plan or have the government serve as third-party administrator for one, and would face a new duty to refer employees to navigators if their coverage is unaffordable or lacks minimum value.

industries.industry: ACA exchange navigators and enrollment-assistance organizations
industries.note: The bill authorizes unlimited appropriations for navigator grants and requires employer referrals of uncovered full-time workers, expanding their funding and role.

analysis.trajectory: With only 5 cosponsors, no Republican support, and three committee referrals with no hearing or markup in over six months, the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress; it would need committee action and floor time that bills of this kind in divided government rarely receive.
